column8: Welcome to Battles of History. Today we are learning about the meh-dak Pocket, in Croatia, from the ninth to the seventeenth of September 1993. Croatian forces attacked a small area of Serb-held villages near the town of gos-pitch. A week later, Canadian and French soldiers of the United Nations came to take it over, and found the villages destroyed. Croatian courts later found that war crimes had been committed there. The people involved remember these days very differently. We will tell you what is known, who says what, and what is still not known. Some chapters describe killings. We tell them plainly and without detail.

meh-dak pocket 1993. On the ninth of September 1993, the Croatian Army and police launched an attack on a Serb-held area south of gos-pitch, in the lee-ka region of Croatia. It was called the meh-dak Pocket. On the fifteenth of September, the two sides agreed to a ceasefire, and to United Nations control of the pocket after the Croatian withdrawal. Canadian and French peacekeepers entered between the fifteenth and the seventeenth of September. They found extensive destruction, and bodies. They also found three survivors, whom they protected and evacuated. In 2008 a court in Zagreb found that war crimes against Serb civilians and prisoners had been committed. It convicted one Croatian commander, and acquitted another.

Croatia and the kra-yee-na. In 1991, Croatia declared independence from Yugoslavia. Many Serbs in Croatia rejected it. With the support of the Yugoslav People's Army, they took control of large areas and declared their own state, the Republic of Serbian kra-yee-na. lee-ka is a high, wooded region of southern Croatia, between the coast mountains and Bosnia. In 1993 the front line ran close to the town of gos-pitch. On this map, Croatian-held areas and Serb-held areas are approximate, as they stood in 1993.

Who is who. The Croatian Army, called the H V, and the special police of Croatia's Interior Ministry. On this page they are red. The kra-yee-na Serb Army, called the S V K, the army of the self-declared Republic of Serbian kra-yee-na. On this page they are blue. The United Nations Protection Force, un-pro-for: here, a Canadian battalion with two French companies. On this page they are white and light blue. The villages also had civilian inhabitants, including elderly people.

Remembered differently. Croatian official commemorations emphasise the operation's military purpose: to end the shelling of gos-pitch. Serb organisations commemorate the victims, and the destroyed villages. Canadian commemorations honour the peacekeepers. The chapters at the end give named, dated examples of each.

How this page tells it. Each line is tagged with where it comes from. An accusation is not a verdict, and a count by an organisation is that organisation's count. The numbers of the dead are on screen, in tables, each with who counted and what they counted. They cannot be added together. This page shows no pictures of the dead, and describes no injuries. No crime excuses another. Both Croats and Serbs in lee-ka suffered crimes in this war.

A war in lee-ka. From 1991, much of inland lee-ka was held by kra-yee-na Serb forces and, at first, the Yugoslav People's Army. Civilians on both sides were driven from their homes, and killed. In 2007, the United Nations tribunal for the former Yugoslavia convicted the kra-yee-na Serb leader mee-lan mar-titch of war crimes and crimes against humanity. Its judgment also found that he took part in an attack on the Croat village of lo-vee-nats in June 1991. In 2003, a court in ree-yeh-ka convicted a Croatian officer, meer-ko no-rats, of crimes against civilians in gos-pitch in 1991, and sentenced him to twelve years. We will meet him again in this story.

The United Nations arrives. A ceasefire in January 1992 opened the way for a United Nations deployment, under the Vance peace plan. The Security Council established the United Nations Protection Force, un-pro-for, on the twenty-first of February 1992. The peacekeeping arrangement was temporary, and did not settle the conflict. The United Nations watched over protected areas, divided into sectors. Some places near the front line, called pink zones, lay just outside them.

A finger of land. South of gos-pitch, a row of small Serb villages reached into Croatian-held land: dee-vo-seh-lo, chit-look, and po-chi-tel, with their hamlets. A United Nations investigation later described it as "a finger of Serb-controlled land jutting into Croat territory". It lay in a pink zone, just outside the protected area called Sector South. Serb organisations call these villages that were under United Nations protection. Outside a designated protected area did not mean outside every United Nations responsibility.

The shelling of gos-pitch. Croatian accounts say that in 1993 the town of gos-pitch was often shelled by kra-yee-na Serb artillery near meh-dak. Croatia's Ministry of Defence presents the operation as a military action to end that threat to gos-pitch.

Early morning, the ninth of September. The Croatian operation was called "jep deh-veh-deh-set tree": Pocket Ninety-Three. The attack began early in the morning of the ninth of September 1993. A United Nations investigation dates it to about six o'clock. According to the tribunal's indictment, the attacking forces included the Croatian Army's 9th Guards Brigade, other army and Home Guard units, and special police of the Interior Ministry. Their exact strength is uncertain. According to the indictment, ra-heem a-deh-mee was the acting commander of the gos-pitch Military District, and meer-ko no-rats commanded the 9th Guards Brigade and a combat group called Sector One. That is the prosecution's description, not a court finding.

The villages taken. Within days, Croatian forces took dee-vo-seh-lo, chit-look and part of po-chi-tel, with their hamlets. Many Serb villagers fled as the attack began. In the Croatian official view, the operation pushed Serb guns back from gos-pitch. How large an area was taken is disputed. Different sources give very different figures, shown on screen.

The people of the pocket. Croatian courts later established that civilians and prisoners of war were killed. The tribunal's indictment also alleged killings of elderly civilians, and of Serb soldiers who had been captured or wounded. The prosecutor's figures are on screen. They are accusations, not verdicts. Other counts, by Serb organisations and others, differ. They are on screen, each with what it counts.

Rockets on Croatian cities. The United Nations reported that kra-yee-na Serb forces fired heavy rockets and missiles at Croatian population centres on the tenth and eleventh of September. Those attacks do not excuse crimes in the pocket, and crimes in the pocket did not excuse them.

An agreement. On the fifteenth of September, the two sides agreed to United Nations control of the pocket after the Croatian withdrawal. The agreement called for a general ceasefire at noon on the fifteenth of September, and for Croatian forces to withdraw to the positions they held before the attack. Serb forces were to stay out. The tribunal's indictment names the signatories: the Croatian general peh-tar stee-peh-titch, and the kra-yee-na Serb general mee-leh no-va-ko-vitch. In a report that December, the United Nations Secretary-General called the operation an incursion by the Croatian Army into the meh-dak pocket.

can-bat One. The United Nations troops in this sector were a Canadian battle group: the Second Battalion, Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry. The UN called it can-bat One. Its commander was Lieutenant-Colonel James Calvin. Two French mechanised companies, from the French battalions freh-bat One and freh-bat Three, served under Canadian command. At the time of the attack, can-bat One was establishing observation posts in the area. Canadian soldiers were wounded in the fighting, and a Canadian officer, Captain Jim deh-coast, died in a vehicle accident during the operation.

The fifteenth of September. On the fifteenth, Canadian C Company and a French company moved forward, to take over the Serb front-line positions. According to the Canadian operational report, Croatian forces fired on the United Nations soldiers "with small arms, heavy machine gun and in some instances 20 mm cannon fire". The report describes repeated exchanges of fire over about fifteen hours, some of them lasting up to ninety minutes. The Canadian report suggested that some Croatian fire may have been in response to Serb sniping at Croatian positions. It says Croatian forces continued firing sporadically at United Nations positions after the sniping stopped.

The roadblock. On the sixteenth of September, the Canadian column was stopped at a Croatian checkpoint. The Canadian report says Lieutenant-Colonel Calvin used the presence of journalists, filming the delays, to press for passage. The barrier was later lifted. Croatian troops withdrew over the sixteenth and seventeenth of September.

What they found. As the peacekeepers entered the villages, they found extensive destruction. Houses and barns had been burned, and they found the bodies of people who had been killed. They also found three survivors, whom they protected and evacuated. Absence from a village does not mean that everyone there died. The Canadians recorded evidence of what they found.

A battle, or not?. Canadian accounts call the fifteenth of September a battle. Veterans Affairs Canada says it is considered by many to be the toughest action faced by Canadian soldiers between the wars in Korea and Afghanistan. What Croatian losses there were in the exchanges, if any, is not known. Figures that circulate are unconfirmed, and this page does not use them.

Accused in The Hague. The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, in The Hague, indicted ra-heem a-deh-mee in 2001. He surrendered, and pleaded not guilty. meer-ko no-rats was indicted later. In 2004 their two cases were joined into one. In 2002 the tribunal also indicted the chief of Croatia's General Staff, General yan-ko bo-bet-ko. He died before trial, and the case ended without a verdict.

Sent to Zagreb. On the fourteenth of September 2005, the tribunal sent the case of a-deh-mee and no-rats to be tried in Croatia. Its referral bench considered that a fair trial and the protection of witnesses could be provided there. It was the first case the tribunal sent to Croatia. The referral was a decision about where to hold the trial, not a verdict. The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, the O S C E, watched the trial for the tribunal's prosecutor.

The verdict. On the thirtieth of May 2008, the County Court in Zagreb acquitted ra-heem a-deh-mee of all charges. It acquitted meer-ko no-rats of ordering the crimes. It convicted him as a commander, for failing to take the action required of him: to prevent crimes by his subordinates, and to punish them. He was sentenced to seven years. According to the tribunal prosecutor's final monitoring report, the findings that were upheld concerned the destruction of property, the mistreatment of prisoners, and the killing of four civilians and two prisoners of war. That was the scope of one man's conviction, not the number killed in the operation. Croatia's Supreme Court heard the appeals in November 2009. In March 2010 it upheld a-deh-mee's acquittal, and reduced no-rats's sentence to six years.

After the verdict. The Zagreb County Court and Croatia's Supreme Court both accepted that war crimes against Serb civilians and prisoners had been committed. The legal argument was about who was responsible. In 2020, Croatia's Supreme Court upheld yo-sip kurm-po-titch's three-year sentence for ordering civilian houses burned. He was acquitted of the allegation that he failed to prevent the killing of four Serb prisoners.

gos-pitch remembers. In September 2026, at the thirty-third anniversary in gos-pitch, officials and veterans attended a mass and a commemorative ceremony. Croatia's Ministry of Defence presents the operation as a military action to protect the town. In September 2023, the Youth Initiative for Human Rights joined a visit to the villages and a commemoration by the Serb National Council. The initiative said that Serb civilian victims were left out of the official state commemorations.

dee-vo-seh-lo remembers. The Serb National Council commemorated the victims in September 2023. In September 2026, the Serb documentation centre Veritas issued an anniversary statement calling for justice. Their remembrance centres on the civilian victims, and on what they see as justice not done. In its 2023 account of a visit, the Youth Initiative for Human Rights described the villages' greatly reduced population.

Canada remembers. In 2023, Canada's Department of National Defence described the battle as a largely forgotten part of Canadian history. On the first of December 2002, the Governor General, Adrienne Clarkson, presented the battle group with the Commander-in-Chief Unit Commendation, for its "courageous and professional execution of duty" in the meh-dak Pocket. Official commemorations in gos-pitch, Serb organisations' memorials, and Canadian honours each tell part of this story. History asks what happened, to whom, and how we know.

In 1993 the front line ran close to the town of gos-pitch. On this map, Croatian-held areas and Serb-held areas are approximate, as they stood in 1993.

It says Croatian forces continued firing sporadically at United Nations positions after the sniping stopped.

The Canadian report says Lieutenant-Colonel Calvin used the presence of journalists, filming the delays, to press for passage. The barrier was later lifted. Croatian troops withdrew over the sixteenth and seventeenth of September.
